raw_summary:
Gemini Decision 1 from Google is now available on AI Gateway. The multimodal decision model works with text, images, audio, video, and PDF documents, returning Boolean probabilities, choices, and scores. Use it to route requests, check policies, filter agent tools, or rank results without generating output tokens.

Use google/gemini-decision-1 with the AI SDK, TypeSafe-compatible API, or Decisions API.

PDF, audio, and video inputs are supported through AI SDK 7. The TypeSafe-compatible and Decisions APIs support text and image inputs.

AI Gateway provides a unified way to access models and track usage and cost. Decision calls appear in logs and count toward budgets alongside other model requests.

See the decision documentation for Choice, Score, and Boolean questions. To pick a decision model, browse the available models or read our decision model guides.

raw_summary:
Gemini Decisions API

Google join Jev and OpenAI in the decision model category with "Gemini Decision 1". This new model API is almost identical to Jev: it supports the same three types of questions (yes/no, choice, and rubric-scoring) and even reuses Jev's term "Noul" for a yes/no question.

It's priced the same as the GPT-6 Luna decision model: 10 cents per million input tokens, and output is free. Jev remains the cheapest of the three, at 4.2 cents per million.

Jev is text (and JSON) only. OpenAI can handle text and images. Gemini Decision 1 is fully multi-model: it covers text, images, audio, video, and PDFs.

I tested it against video by passing these questions to it along with my Yonkers stomping robot video file:

dragon: Does this video have a dragon in it?
robot: Does this video have a robot in it?
france: Is this video set in France?
usa: Is this video set in the USA?

Jev and OpenAI both return 1.0 or 0.0 for yes/no questions, but Gemini insists on being a little less confident than that:

{
  "dragon": {
    "type": "yes_no",
    "probability": 0.04976021841520312
  },
  "robot": {
    "type": "yes_no",
    "probability": 0.9234055387792485
  },
  "france": {
    "type": "yes_no",
    "probability": 0.08329171353166241
  },
  "usa": {
    "type": "yes_no",
    "probability": 0.9230459995157706
  }
}

Via Hacker News

aws-emulator

Finally, an official emulator from AWS to run tests against a local clone of their many different services without having to provision a paid API key to do so.

It's written in Rust by a huge swarm of agents - 29,684 commits in the first three weeks of the project. Swaminathan (Swami) Sivasubramanian wrote about how it came to be in a guest post on Werner Vogels' blog.

It currently requires Docker to run on macOS or Windows. I'm hoping they fix that in the future - it would be great if you could download a single binary and use that as part of a standard test suite in other languages and on other platforms.

raw_summary:
Anthropic's IPO roadshow video

Anthropic kicked off their IPO roadshow yesterday, and their roadshow video has some previously unreleased information about how their business works.

The section on "Approach to compute" with co-founder Tom Brown is particularly interesting, describing how Anthropic train and serve Claude across AWS Trainium, Google TPUs, NVIDIA GPUs, and AMD GPUs.

I'm not sure why there's no official video transcript, but here's one that I extracted using MacWhisper. Highlights below:

We train and serve Claude now across all four major chip families. That's only possible because early on we made an unconventional bet on a multi-chip strategy. At the time, many people thought that running AI models on different chips wasn't worth the effort. Each chip needs its own tailored software stack and inference stack, which is expensive and difficult to build. We've now been doing it for years, and we've gotten incredibly good at it. [...]

As an example, this year, we started working with AMD GPUs for the first time. In the past, bringing on a new chip platform took dozens of engineers months of work This time, we had Mythos try it out. It got Claude running on AMD in just three days, with basically no human intervention. Claude ported or wrote almost 100% of the kernels. [...]

The second driver of our compute advantage is our rate of discovery of compute multipliers. We focus on total effective compute, which is the multiplicative product of physical capacity times the compute multipliers that we discover. Each one we discover makes our pool of total effective compute bigger. For example, say you need 100 units of compute to train a model of a certain intelligence. A 4x compute multiplier means you can use 25 units of compute to train the exact same model. Or you can use those hundred physical units to train an even more intelligent model that would have previously required 400 units.

Compute multipliers create a competitive advantage for us that's hard to replicate. They build on each other. Each new multiplier we discover has a positive effect on the multipliers before it. They stack. We believe that this can accelerate even further as we approach recursive self-improvement. Claude will be able to discover compute multipliers entirely by itself, allowing the number of compute multipliers to grow faster and faster.

We got a hint at Anthropic's multi-chip strategy last September in their postmortem of three recent issues, where they described bugs that affected just their TPU deployments.

analysis.summary_cn: Google Cloud 在 AlloyDB AI 中预览 ai.classify 与 ai.extract 两个 SQL 函数，直接在 PostgreSQL 18 内调用 Gemini 完成文本分类与结构化抽取，省去导出数据、外部调用、解析响应等应用侧循环。官方称配合智能批处理可支撑生产规模，降低延迟、token 成本与数据跨网络合规风险，扩展版本需 1.6.1 以上。

raw_summary:
Transactional databases store vast amounts of unstructured text — clinical notes, customer reviews, support tickets, invoices, and property descriptions. Historically, working with this text meant building complex application code: You had to export data from the database, call external model endpoints, write custom prompt wrappers, parse unpredictable responses, manage retry logic, and update database records. This application-side loop creates operational friction. It introduces query latency, bloats application code, increases model token costs, and creates data compliance risks by moving sensitive information across multiple network boundaries.

We built AlloyDB AI to bring Gemini world knowledge directly into your operational database. Rather than treating artificial intelligence as a disconnected external service, we integrated model intelligence directly into the database engine. Today, we are announcing the preview of two new SQL functions in the AlloyDB AI query engine — ai.classify and ai.extract — available in the google_ml_integration extension (version 1.6.1 or later) on PostgreSQL 18, allowing you to perform classification and structured extraction directly inside your database using standard SQL. Supported by smart batching for AI functions (previously known as AI Function Acceleration), these functions deliver production scalability and performance. 

Now, let’s take a look at these new functions and how to use them.

Classifying text directly in SQL with ai.classify

The ai.classify function categorizes text into user-defined classes without requiring manual prompt engineering. You can specify categories as a simple list of labels or provide a list containing label names and descriptions to guide model context.

Key capabilities include:

  • Single-label classification (output_mode => 'single') to assign the single best category

  • Multi-label classification (output_mode => 'multi') to return all matching categories

  • Category descriptions using 2D arrays to provide explicit context for each label

  • Few-shot prompting by supplying inline examples

  • Flexible execution modes for individual rows (TEXT), arrays (TEXT[]), and cursors (REFCURSOR)

Here’s a quick example showing how you can classify customer feedback directly within a SQL query:

code_block
<ListValue: [StructValue([('code', "SET google_ml_integration.enable_preview_ai_functions = TRUE;\r\n\r\nCREATE TABLE product_reviews (id INT, review TEXT);\r\n\r\nINSERT INTO product_reviews VALUES\r\n(1, 'Fantastic, would buy again!'),\r\n(2, 'Broken on arrival.'),\r\n(3, 'Mediocre, not worth the price.');\r\n\r\nSELECT unnest(\r\n ai.classify(\r\n inputs => ARRAY(SELECT review FROM product_reviews ORDER BY id),\r\n categories => ARRAY[\r\n ['positive', 'Good sentiment'],\r\n ['neutral', 'Neither good nor bad sentiment'],\r\n ['negative', 'Bad sentiment']\r\n ],\r\n batch_size => 5\r\n )\r\n) AS sentiment;\r\n\r\n-- Expected Output:\r\n-- sentiment\r\n-- ---------\r\n-- positive\r\n-- negative\r\n-- negative"), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7fd0a72fe290>)])]>

Extracting structured JSON with ai.extract

The ai.extract function transforms unstructured text into structured JSON data matching your target schema — specified as a JSON schema or a text list of fields. It handles system instructions internally, saving you from writing prompt templates or response parsers.

Key capabilities include:

  • Schema flexibility supporting standard JSON schemas or plain text field lists

  • Automatic transformation of unstructured text into machine-readable JSON

  • Overloaded function signatures for single rows, arrays, and cursor batching

Here’s an example extracting clinical fields from free-form medical notes:

code_block
<ListValue: [StructValue([('code', 'SET google_ml_integration.enable_preview_ai_functions = TRUE;\r\n\r\nSELECT ai.extract( \r\n input => \'Patient Jane Smith, 52 years old, visited the clinic on Oct 25. She is currently experiencing a mild fever, persistent cough, and severe body aches. The doctor prescribed Ibuprofen and Amoxicillin.\',\r\n output_schema => \'{\r\n "patient_name": {"type": "string"},\r\n "age": {"type": "integer"},\r\n "symptoms": {\r\n "type": "array",\r\n "items": {"type": "string"}\r\n },\r\n "prescribed_medications": {\r\n "type": "array",\r\n "items": {"type": "string"}\r\n }\r\n }\'\r\n);\r\n\r\n--- Expected output \r\n-- {\r\n-- "patient_name": "Jane Smith",\r\n-- "age": 52,\r\n-- "symptoms": [\r\n-- "mild fever",\r\n-- "persistent cough",\r\n-- "severe body aches"\r\n-- ],\r\n-- "prescribed_medications": [\r\n-- "Ibuprofen",\r\n-- "Amoxicillin"\r\n-- ]\r\n-- }'), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7fd0a72f1010>)])]>

Speeding up queries with smart batching

Running AI evaluations row-by-row can slow down query execution. AlloyDB addresses this with smart batching for AI functions. When you use ai.classify or ai.extract in SQL WHERE clause expressions, the database engine automatically groups inputs into optimized micro-batches before sending them to Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform models.

Smart batching delivers significant performance and efficiency improvements:

  • Faster inference for query execution compared to row-at-a-time evaluations

  • Reduces total model token spend by optimizing input prompt overhead

Real-world industry applications

Native classification and extraction functions support operational workflows across key industry sectors:

  • Healthcare: Securely convert free-text clinical notes into structured records containing patient names, symptoms, and prescribed medications, keeping patient data safely within the confines of the database.

  • Financial services: Extract vendor details, invoice dates, and line-item totals from scanned document text.

  • Legal technology: Pull governing law, liability caps, and termination notice periods from contract documents.

  • Real estate: Extract property types, bedroom counts, and price ranges from descriptive listing text.

  • Knowledge graphs: Extract entities and relationships from documents to populate PostgreSQL Property Graph (PGQ) structures.

Next steps and getting started

We are continuing to expand in-database AI capabilities in AlloyDB, with upcoming enhancements planned for advanced cost optimization, line-level provenance tracking, and query pushdowns beyond WHERE clauses.

To start using ai.classify and ai.extract in your database:

  • Review the AlloyDB AI Query Engine documentation.

  • Explore the AlloyDB release notes.
source: Google Cloud AI and Machine Learning Blog
title: Introducing new AI functions for AlloyDB: ai.classify and ai.extract

raw_summary:
It just got easier to prove your expertise in building production-ready agents. Today, Google Cloud is introducing the Professional Agentic Architect certification as the latest milestone in our Gemini Agent Ready (GEAR) initiative. Nearly one million developers are using GEAR to skill up on agents, but what makes this particular certification so special is its adoption within Google’s walls.

Over the past four months, Google Cloud has trained thousands of forward deployed engineers and strategic partners on our own advanced curriculum. Originally built as an internal training initiative, we are now opening it up to the entire developer community and partner ecosystem through this new certification. 

As the VP who manages our forward-deployed engineers here at Google Cloud (Ravi) and the managing director of Google Cloud learning (Gary), we’ve seen just how effective this program has been inside Google at helping our teams rethink the way they build, deploy, and use AI in everyday in almost every way. We’re equally about what this new certification can bring to everyone — developers, engineers, and anyone else ready to demonstrate their agentic leadership.

A new hybrid format to validate your real-world skills

This is not a traditional multiple choice exam. Google has introduced a new hybrid format that requires you to prove both conceptual know-how and hands-on execution.

  1. Part 1 (The multiple choice proctored exam): Evaluates your system design choices, architectural standards, cost optimization, and security governance.

  2. Part 2 (Hands-on labs on Google Skills): Puts you in an active cloud environment to build, test, and debug live agentic workflows.

Why earning this certification can help advance your career

As enterprises look to find top AI talent, this certification immediately signals that you have the advanced skills necessary to design secure, governed, and high-performance multi-agent systems. 

Our research with Ipsos on AI skill building shows that certifications drive more recruiter outreach: 82% of learners using Google Skills say that mentioning Google Cloud certifications on their resume drives more recruiter responses.

And it’s not just about getting the call — it’s about being able to answer it. That same research showed that 90% of cloud professionals say credentials like Google Cloud certifications give them the verified know-how needed to fill in-demand roles. 

What’s covered on the exam

The certification validates your proficiency across five key domains:

  1. Build agents using low-code tools (democratizing rapid agent prototyping).

  2. Use coding agents for application development (supercharging your coding productivity).

  3. Develop custom agents on the Gemini platform with open source frameworks.

  4. Evaluate and deploy agentic workflows (monitoring, optimizing, and ensuring performance).

  5. Secure and govern agentic workflows (protecting sensitive enterprise data and ensuring model safety).

Battle-tested by thousands of Google Cloud engineers and partners — now available to you

Enterprise demand for agentic workloads has skyrocketed. As our customers move past AI prompting and run their most business critical workloads on Google Cloud, we’ve built our own team that delivers the agentic future with them — at scale. Google Cloud partners and Google’s forward deployed engineers are embedded directly with customers around the world and are prepared to solve deep technical challenges because of this rigorous curriculum and certification.

While building our forward-deployed engineering program, we wanted to standardize training and upskilling for customers, Google Cloud partners, and our own engineers with the Professional Agentic Architect certification. This ensures our own teams are using the same world-class standards that we recommend to our customers and partners, allowing us to learn from each other and sharpen our skills together. 

Skill up for your certification at no cost today

  1. Register for Gemini Agent Ready to get access to 35 free monthly learning credits on Google Skills. For Google Cloud customers, Get Certified provides a cohort-based, guided certification journey at no cost. 

  2. For Google Cloud partners, register for Partner Certification Kickstart and review the partner learning path.

  3. Review the exam guide, learning path and sample questions.

  4. Get hands-on with Google Skills labs and preparation modules to get comfortable developing custom agents on Gemini platform with open source frameworks. 

  5. Register for the multiple-choice exam, complete the hands-on lab requirements, and claim your digital badge to showcase your expertise to the world.

Don't just prompt AI — architect it. Get certified today.
source: Google Cloud AI and Machine Learning Blog
title: Don’t just prompt AI — architect it: Introducing the Professional Agentic Architect Certification
